purpose: Documents full-text editorial review of newly downloaded posts before canonical ingestion.

posts.title: More on Jesus’ Upbringing
posts.author: BDEhrman
posts.description: Reconstructs Jesus’ upbringing by examining evidence for his parents, siblings, working-class background, language, education, and otherwise undocumented early life.
posts.searchSummary: Reconstructs what can probably be known about Jesus before his public ministry from early, independently attested traditions. It examines Joseph’s work as a lower-class laborer, Mary and Jesus’ siblings, and evidence that Jesus spoke Aramaic and may have learned to read Hebrew despite limited schooling. The post concludes that little else is historically secure about his childhood before his adult baptism by John.

posts.title: The Early Life of Jesus
posts.author: BDEhrman
posts.description: Explains how historical criteria distinguish traditions about Jesus’ childhood, arguing that he was raised in Nazareth within a Jewish family.
posts.searchSummary: Introduces the historical criteria scholars use to separate probable events in Jesus’ early life from legendary Gospel stories, including independent attestation, dissimilarity, and historical credibility. Applying those methods, Ehrman argues that Jesus was raised in the small Galilean village of Nazareth, despite Matthew’s and Luke’s preference for Bethlehem. He also treats Jesus’ Jewish upbringing as firmly established across the earliest traditions.
topics: Methods for Studying the Historical Jesus

posts.title: Platinum Lecture on September 20
posts.author: jennao
posts.description: Announces the September 20 Platinum-member Zoom lecture, with its subject forthcoming and a recording planned for members unable to attend.
posts.searchSummary: Announces the next quarterly Zoom lecture for Platinum blog members, scheduled for September 20 at 3:00 p.m. Eastern. The topic had not yet been finalized, but the notice provides private access information and invites members to bring questions for the closing discussion. A recording would be distributed afterward to members unable to attend the live event.

posts.title: My Odd Situation, Writing this Book…
posts.author: BDEhrman
posts.description: Reflects on researching a book about Jesus and modern economics without a predetermined thesis, contrasting this uncertainty with Ehrman’s usual writing process.
posts.searchSummary: Describes Ehrman’s unusually open-ended research process for a proposed book examining Jesus, wealth, and modern economic systems. Unlike earlier projects that began with a settled thesis, this one requires substantial reading in economic history, ancient Galilean society, prosperity preaching, and Jesus’ teachings about money before he knows his argument. He suggests that Luke 16:9 may eventually provide a direction but emphasizes that the conclusion remains unsettled.

posts.title: How the World Was Created in 4004 BCE
posts.author: BDEhrman
posts.description: Explains how James Ussher calculated creation in 4004 BCE from biblical genealogies and why his chronology influenced Christian literalism.
posts.searchSummary: Traces the familiar claim that creation occurred in 4004 BCE to Archbishop James Ussher’s seventeenth-century calculations from biblical genealogies and ancient chronology. It explains how the six days of creation, 2 Peter’s equation of a divine day with a thousand years, and calendar problems shaped a six-thousand-year timetable. The post notes that this scheme influenced Western Christian Bibles but would have predicted the world’s end in 1997.

posts.title: Hebrew Bible/English Old Testament: Charting Their Differences
posts.author: BDEhrman
posts.description: Compares the contents and organization of the Hebrew Bible and Christian Old Testaments, explaining their differing book counts, orders, and canons.
posts.searchSummary: Compares how the same core scriptures are counted and arranged in the Protestant Old Testament and the Hebrew Bible. It explains the Tanakh’s divisions into Torah, Prophets, and Writings, contrasting its twenty-four-book count with the Protestant thirty-nine-book organization. The post also charts deuterocanonical books included in Roman Catholic and Orthodox Old Testaments but excluded from both the Hebrew Bible and Protestant canon.
